title: N-Queens
description: Brute force to optimized: validating complete assignments at the end versus row-by-row backtracking with immediate O(1) conflict pruning.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer n, return all distinct ways to place n queens on an n by n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other (no two share a row, column, or diagonal). Each solution is represented as a list of strings, where "Q" marks a queen and "." marks an empty space.

blocks.text: Since no two queens can share a row, exactly one queen must be placed in each of the n rows. The task reduces to choosing, for each row in turn, a column that does not conflict with any queen already placed in an earlier row, via a shared column or a shared diagonal.

blocks.title: Analogy: Seating Guests Who Cannot See Each Other
blocks.text: Picture seating one guest per row of a theater, where guests seated along the same column, or along a diagonal line of sight, would be uncomfortable. This problem asks for every way to seat one guest per row so no two share a column or diagonal line of sight.

blocks.caption: One queen per row is forced; only column and diagonal conflicts need checking against earlier rows

blocks.text: Before considering full-board placements, notice that placing queens row by row, and immediately rejecting any column that conflicts with an already-placed queen, avoids ever exploring a branch that is already invalid, the essence of backtracking with pruning.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since one queen must occupy each row, the recursion can proceed row by row: at row r, try every column, and recurse to row r+1 only for columns that do not conflict with previously placed queens.

Observation 2: A column conflict is simply "has this column index already been used by an earlier row." A same-diagonal conflict (top-left to bottom-right) occurs when (row - col) is the same for two queens; a same-anti-diagonal conflict (top-right to bottom-left) occurs when (row + col) is the same for two queens.

Observation 3: Maintaining three sets, used columns, used (row-col) diagonal identifiers, and used (row+col) anti-diagonal identifiers, lets each conflict check happen in O(1), avoiding the need to scan previously placed queens explicitly.

Observation 4: The base case is reaching row n, meaning n queens have been successfully placed with no conflicts, at which point the current board configuration is a valid solution to record.

This leads to backtracking row by row, tracking used columns, used (row-col) diagonals, and used (row+col) anti-diagonals in three sets, skipping any column that conflicts, and recording the board once all n rows are filled.
A more literal brute force would try every combination of n column choices (one per row) and check all pairwise attacks at the end, rather than pruning as soon as a conflict is found.

items: Try every combination of column choices for each row (n^n combinations in the most naive framing).
For each complete assignment, check every pair of queens for row, column, or diagonal conflicts.
Keep only assignments with no conflicts at all.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Generating every combination of column assignments first, then validating only at the end, wastes enormous effort exploring branches that are already invalid partway through.
Checking all pairs for conflicts, rather than checking a new queen only against already-placed ones during construction, repeats work.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^n times n squared) in the worst framing, generating all combinations and checking all pairs.
Space: O(n) recursion depth, plus O(n squared) for storing combinations before filtering.

Limitation: exploring full assignments before checking validity wastes enormous effort on invalid partial placements; pruning immediately upon detecting a conflict (during row-by-row placement) avoids ever completing an invalid branch.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why immediate pruning matters: as soon as placing a queen in a given row/column conflicts with any earlier queen, every possible completion of that branch is guaranteed invalid, so there is no reason to place any further queens down that path.

What to track for O(1) conflict checks: a set of used columns; a set of used (row - col) values (identifying which diagonal each queen occupies); a set of used (row + col) values (identifying which anti-diagonal each queen occupies).

How the recursion proceeds: at row r, for each column c not in any of the three used sets, place the queen (add to all three sets), recurse to row r+1, then remove it from all three sets (undo) before trying the next column.

The core idea: prune illegal branches the moment a conflict is detected, using O(1) set membership checks, instead of validating a complete assignment only at the very end.

Backtrack row by row, using three sets (columns, diagonals via row-col, anti-diagonals via row+col) to check conflicts in O(1) per column tried, recording the board once all n rows are successfully filled.
Dry run for n = 4 (first solution found)

blocks.caption: Backtrack row by row; use sets for columns and both diagonal directions to skip conflicting columns instantly

codes.python:
def solve_n_queens(n):
    result = []
    cols, diag1, diag2 = set(), set(), set()   # diag1: row-col, diag2: row+col
    board = [['.'] * n for _ in range(n)]

    def backtrack(row):
        if row == n:
            result.append([''.join(r) for r in board])
            return
        for col in range(n):
            if col in cols or (row - col) in diag1 or (row + col) in diag2:
                continue                                  # pruned: conflict detected immediately
            cols.add(col); diag1.add(row - col); diag2.add(row + col)
            board[row][col] = 'Q'
            backtrack(row + 1)
            board[row][col] = '.'
            cols.remove(col); diag1.remove(row - col); diag2.remove(row + col)   # undo

    backtrack(0)
    return result

blocks.text: Because exactly one queen occupies each row, the search only needs to choose a column per row, and the three sets (columns, row-col diagonals, row+col anti-diagonals) fully capture every possible conflict a new queen could have with any previously placed queen, in O(1) per check. Pruning invalid columns immediately, rather than after completing a full assignment, means the search never wastes time exploring a branch that is already doomed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n!) in the worst case (bounded further by pruning in practice), since each row narrows the valid columns.
Space: O(n) for the three sets and the board, plus recursion depth.

blocks.text: N-Queens is the canonical example of constraint-satisfaction backtracking with immediate pruning: placing one queen per row and rejecting conflicting columns instantly, rather than validating only complete assignments.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "place items with row/column/diagonal constraints", think: backtrack row by row, track conflicts with O(1) sets, prune immediately.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unpruned brute force is astronomically slower; the row-by-row backtracking approach with O(1) conflict sets runs in O(n!) worst-case time (heavily pruned in practice) and O(n) space.

items: Pattern: row-by-row backtracking with immediate pruning via O(1) conflict-tracking sets.
Core Idea: track used columns, row-col diagonals, and row+col anti-diagonals; skip any column already conflicting; recurse row by row; record a solution when all n rows are filled.
Time: O(n^n times n squared) for the unpruned brute force, O(n!) worst case (pruned in practice) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: pruning a conflicting branch the instant it is detected avoids wasting time on any doomed continuation.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, canonical backtracking-with-pruning problem.
One line memory trick: one queen per row; track columns and both diagonals; skip conflicts instantly.
